misconceptions.statement: Sweet is tasted only at the tip of the tongue and bitter only at the back.
misconceptions.why: The old tongue-map diagram in books is shown as fact.
misconceptions.fix: All basic tastes can be sensed on every part of the tongue that has taste buds. The tongue map is a myth.

probe.question: Where on the tongue can you taste bitter food?
probe.wrong_answer: Only at the back of the tongue.

misconceptions.root_belief: a simplified diagram is the whole truth
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of common myths in biology textbooks and taste-perception research

misconceptions.statement: Spicy hotness is a taste detected by taste buds, like sweet and salty.
misconceptions.why: In everyday language we say food 'tastes hot'.
misconceptions.fix: Spicy hotness is sensed as pain or heat by nerve endings, not by taste buds. Taste buds detect sweet, sour, salty, bitter and umami.

probe.question: Which sense detects the burning of a green chilli?
probe.wrong_answer: Taste buds, because chilli has a spicy taste.

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

misconceptions.statement: A completely dry tongue can taste dry sugar crystals just as well.
misconceptions.why: Students do not notice saliva's role in everyday eating.
misconceptions.fix: Taste buds respond only to substances dissolved in liquid such as saliva. A dry tongue tastes little.

probe.question: Why can't you taste a dry sugar crystal on a dried tongue immediately?
probe.wrong_answer: You can, saliva makes no difference to taste.

misconceptions.root_belief: what you cannot see does not matter

misconceptions.statement: Skin is just a single thin covering with nothing inside it.
misconceptions.why: Only the outer surface of the skin can be seen.
misconceptions.fix: Skin has layers: the thin outer epidermis and the thicker dermis below it, which contains nerves, blood vessels and glands.

probe.question: How many layers does skin have and what is inside it?
probe.wrong_answer: One layer, just a covering with nothing in it.

misconceptions.root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist

misconceptions.statement: The outer visible layer of skin holds the nerves that feel touch.
misconceptions.why: Touch seems to happen right at the surface.
misconceptions.fix: Many receptors and nerve endings sit in the dermis and the lower epidermis, deeper than the dead surface cells.

probe.question: Where are most touch receptors found: in the outermost dead cells or deeper in the skin?
probe.wrong_answer: In the outermost visible layer.

misconceptions.root_belief: the visible surface is the working part

misconceptions.statement: Skin has only one kind of receptor that feels everything, hot, cold and touch alike.
misconceptions.why: All feelings seem to arrive through the same skin.
misconceptions.fix: Skin has different receptors for light touch, pressure, heat, cold and pain.

probe.question: How does skin tell hot from cold?
probe.wrong_answer: One kind of receptor feels both; the brain just guesses.

misconceptions.root_belief: one organ has one single mechanism

misconceptions.statement: Pain is just a very strong touch.
misconceptions.why: Pressing harder and harder eventually hurts.
misconceptions.fix: Pain has its own receptors; a very hard press activates both pressure receptors and pain receptors.

probe.question: Is pain a stronger form of touch or a separate sense?
probe.wrong_answer: Just very strong touch.

misconceptions.root_belief: more intensity of the same thing

misconceptions.statement: Every part of the skin is equally sensitive to touch.
misconceptions.why: Skin feels uniform from the outside.
misconceptions.fix: Fingertips, lips and tongue have many receptors and are very sensitive; the back and thighs have fewer.

probe.question: Which can tell two close pin points apart better: fingertip or back?
probe.wrong_answer: Both are equally good.

misconceptions.root_belief: all parts of a thing behave the same
misconceptions.source_hint: classroom studies using the two-point discrimination activity

misconceptions.statement: The back is more sensitive than the fingertip because it has a larger area of skin.
misconceptions.why: Bigger area is assumed to mean more feeling.
misconceptions.fix: Sensitivity depends on how closely receptors are packed, not on area. Fingertips pack many more per square centimetre.

probe.question: Why is a fingertip more sensitive than the back?
probe.wrong_answer: The back is larger so it feels more.

misconceptions.root_belief: bigger or more means more effect

misconceptions.statement: We smell with the outer visible part of the nose.
misconceptions.why: The nose is seen only from the outside.
misconceptions.fix: Smell receptors are in a patch high inside the nasal cavity; the outer nose just channels air to them.

probe.question: Where are smell receptors located?
probe.wrong_answer: On the outside skin of the nose.

misconceptions.root_belief: the visible part is the whole organ

misconceptions.statement: Smell needs nothing to reach the nose; we sense it from a distance without particles.
misconceptions.why: Smell spreads invisibly so there seems to be no physical carrier.
misconceptions.fix: We smell because tiny particles of a substance float in the air and reach the smell receptors.

probe.question: Why can you smell food cooking in another room?
probe.wrong_answer: Smell is a feeling that needs no particles to travel.

misconceptions.root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist
misconceptions.source_hint: research on children's particle ideas about gases and diffusion

misconceptions.statement: Flavour of food is sensed only by the tongue; the nose has nothing to do with it.
misconceptions.why: We put food in the mouth, so the tongue gets all the credit.
misconceptions.fix: Flavour comes from taste and smell together; much of what we call taste is actually smell.

probe.question: Why does an onion taste different if you pinch your nose?
probe.wrong_answer: It should not; the tongue alone tastes it.

misconceptions.root_belief: one event has one single cause
misconceptions.source_hint: common misconceptions listed in school physiology teaching literature

misconceptions.statement: Food tastes bland with a cold because mucus covers the tongue and blocks the taste buds.
misconceptions.why: A blocked nose and a 'coated' mouth both feel unpleasant.
misconceptions.fix: Taste buds still work; food seems bland because the blocked nose stops smell signals reaching the brain.

probe.question: Why does food taste dull when your nose is blocked?
probe.wrong_answer: Mucus blocks the taste buds on the tongue.

misconceptions.root_belief: the effect is where the blockage is felt

misconceptions.statement: The visible ear flap is the whole ear and where hearing happens.
misconceptions.why: Only the outer ear is visible.
misconceptions.fix: The pinna only collects sound; the eardrum, middle ear and inner ear inside the head do the rest.

probe.question: What does the outer ear flap do?
probe.wrong_answer: It hears the sound.

misconceptions.root_belief: the visible part is the whole organ

misconceptions.statement: Sound itself travels along a nerve from the ear to the brain.
misconceptions.why: We think of a message as the same thing that started out.
misconceptions.fix: The ear changes vibrations into electrical signals in nerves; sound as vibration does not travel in nerves.

probe.question: What travels along the nerve from the ear to the brain?
probe.wrong_answer: The sound itself.

misconceptions.root_belief: the thing travels unchanged all the way
misconceptions.source_hint: research on student ideas about sense transduction and sound

misconceptions.statement: The ear alone does the hearing; the brain has no role.
misconceptions.why: The ear is the named organ of hearing.
misconceptions.fix: The ear detects vibrations, but the brain interprets the signals as sound.

probe.question: If the nerve from the ear to the brain is cut, can the ear still give the sense of hearing?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the ear itself hears.

misconceptions.root_belief: the sense organ alone does the sensing

misconceptions.statement: Sound can travel through empty space.
misconceptions.why: Films show explosions in space with loud noise.
misconceptions.fix: Sound needs a medium such as air, water or a solid; it cannot travel in a vacuum.

probe.question: Can astronauts hear each other directly in outer space without radios?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, sound travels in empty space.

misconceptions.root_belief: effects need no carrier
misconceptions.source_hint: research on children's ideas about sound propagation

misconceptions.statement: Air moves all the way from the speaker to our ear carrying the sound.
misconceptions.why: Wind and breath move air, so sound is imagined to be moved air.
misconceptions.fix: Air particles only vibrate to and fro; the vibration passes on, but the air does not travel to the ear.

probe.question: Does the air near a drum travel to your ear when you hear it?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the same air travels to the ear.

misconceptions.root_belief: the carrier moves along with the effect
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of student models of sound as a substance moving through air

misconceptions.statement: The ear is only for hearing; balance is sensed by the eyes and legs.
misconceptions.why: Ears are always introduced as the organ of hearing.
misconceptions.fix: The inner ear also holds fluid-filled canals that sense head movement and position and help balance.

probe.question: Why can an ear infection make a person dizzy?
probe.wrong_answer: It cannot; balance has nothing to do with the ear.

misconceptions.root_belief: one organ has one job

misconceptions.statement: Reflex actions are controlled by the brain like a very quick thought.
misconceptions.why: All body control is thought to pass through the brain.
misconceptions.fix: In many reflexes, the spinal cord responds before the message reaches the brain.

probe.question: Which part decides when you pull your hand from a hot pan?
probe.wrong_answer: The brain decides very quickly.

misconceptions.root_belief: all body control goes through the brain
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of student understanding of the nervous system

misconceptions.statement: Any quick action, like catching a ball, is a reflex.
misconceptions.why: Reflex is used in everyday language for good reactions.
misconceptions.fix: A reflex is automatic and does not need thought. Catching a ball is a learned, voluntary action even if quick.

probe.question: Is catching a ball a reflex action?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because it is very fast.

misconceptions.root_belief: fast means automatic

misconceptions.statement: Sneezing and blinking are voluntary because we can do or stop them when we want.
misconceptions.why: We can sometimes override these actions.
misconceptions.fix: Sneezing and blinking happen automatically; being able to control them sometimes does not make them voluntary.

probe.question: Is a sneeze voluntary or involuntary?
probe.wrong_answer: Voluntary, because I can hold it back.

misconceptions.root_belief: sometimes controllable means always controlled

misconceptions.statement: Pain is always felt exactly where the damage is.
misconceptions.why: Everyday pain such as a cut hurts where it happens.
misconceptions.fix: In referred pain, the brain feels pain in a different place from the real problem, such as heart trouble causing arm pain.

probe.question: A person has pain in the left arm during a heart attack; where is the problem?
probe.wrong_answer: In the left arm itself.

misconceptions.root_belief: the effect appears where the cause is
misconceptions.source_hint: medical education literature on referred pain

misconceptions.statement: Pain is created in the injured body part itself, not in the brain.
misconceptions.why: The hurt part seems to feel the pain.
misconceptions.fix: The injured part sends signals; the brain produces the feeling of pain and places it on the body.

probe.question: Where is the feeling of pain actually produced?
probe.wrong_answer: In the injured part, like the toe.

misconceptions.root_belief: the feeling happens where the sense organ is
